Title: Defending Against Prompt Injection with DataFilter
Abstract: When large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to automate tasks and interact with untrusted external data, prompt injection emerges as a significant security threat. By injecting malicious instructions into the data that LLMs access, an attacker can arbitrarily override the original user task and redirect the agent toward unintended, potentially harmful actions. Existing defenses either require access to model weights (fine-tuning), incur substantial utility loss (detection-based), or demand non-trivial system redesign (system-level). Motivated by this, we propose Data Filter, a test-time model-agnostic defense that removes malicious instructions from the data before it reaches the backend LLM. Data Filter is trained with supervised fine-tuning on simulated injections and leverages both the user’s instruction and the data to selectively strip adversarial content while preserving benign information. Across multiple benchmarks, Data Filter consistently reduces the prompt injection attack success rates to near zero while maintaining the LLMs’ utility. Data Filter delivers strong security, high utility, and plug-and-play deployment, making it a strong practical defense to secure black-box commercial LLMs against prompt injection. Our Data Filter model is released here for immediate use, with the code to reproduce our results here.
Major_Contribution_Result: DataFilter is a test-time, model-agnostic defense that strips malicious instructions from untrusted data before they reach a backend LLM, trained with SFT on simulated injections using both user instruction and data context. Across benchmarks, authors report ASRs reduced to near zero while preserving utility; on SEP, DataFilter keeps ASRs in low single digits across six attacks for gpt-4o and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (e.g., Context ASR 2.2%/2.6%), outperforming several detection and prompting baselines.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Authors state: (1) extra inference overhead per untrusted data item; (2) cannot defend strong optimization-based adaptive attacks that break existing defenses; (3) developers must supply a concise user command (very long user messages degrade filtering); false negatives can occur when injections closely match legitimate task content, and false positives on imperative benign text (e.g., recipes).
Critics: Practical plug-in defense for black-box backends with strong reported SEP/AgentDojo-style results. Limitations around adaptive attacks and long prompts are material for agent deployments. It filters data rather than securing tool control flow, so it complements—not replaces—system-level designs like capability/IFC approaches.
